text:
They crouch down to pick up the datacore, tossing it to you underarm. "Well, Captain $playerFirstName, I suspect you have a new quest," Gargoyle's arms cross with a satisfied look, "I think I'll be seeing you on the Holo-feeds when people find out about this project, so go have fun!"

Their tone shifts slightly. "Now get out of my office! I have a new toy to play with!"

Recovered - Penrose-class Specifications

Universally all Planetkiller Device deployments that have occurred in the Persean Sector post-collapse were performed by conventional warships in orbit of the target. While this is effective, as Opis and Hanan Pacha prove, it is a perversion of usual operating procedure and vulnerable to interception. The Planetkiller Device was originally intended to be deployed by the DISPP-974C Interfector Missile, designed by Consolidated Mysore-Congreve.

The benefit of this approach is obvious, the DISPP-974C is the largest phase capable object ever devised, it's immense flux capacitors allow it to remain phased semi-permanently, making interception of its payload, functionally impossible. This assured destruction makes the threat of a Planetkiller much more serious, and the construction of this Deployment Vehicle is a gun pointed at the head of the Persean Sector.

Unfortunately an automatic failsafe will not allow launch without a Planetkiller Device installed and unsafed by the paired authorization codes. Use of the DISPP-974C for conventional bombardment is therefore impossible.

The loss of this installation was the greatest strategic defeat our faction has ever endured. Luckily without the authorization codes its new owners cannot make use of it anymore than we could. 

Retaking it should be our top military priority, not for the object itself, but what it represents.

Your comms officer responds to the order with trepidation, likely internalising the gravity of the request, and establishes a link to the base commander in charge of the Planetkiller Launch Site. There is an almost giddy excitement to the commander when he answers the connection, maybe it's a good thing there are no authorization codes to give him, he would be too eager to have them.

"$PlayerSirOrMadam, this is Base Commander Calhoum, the ball is green. We are ready to launch at your command, just give the word."

There is an edge to the call-and-response you can overhear behind him in the Tactical Centre, a cramped, spartan and heavily reinforced room hidden in a classified location. It seems the commander's coworkers do not share his enthusiasm in being party to sundering a world. A few members of your bridge crew appear to hold their breath in anticipation of your next order, you catch your targeting officer mumble a faint prayer.
options: jdp_missile_2:"That's a negative Commander, stand down."

text:
Surprisingly, the base commander does not seem at all disappointed, maybe they aren't as much of a war-hawk as they appear. You overhear someone release their breath behind you.

"Orders confirmed, standing down $playerSirOrMadam, I repeat, standing down."

You stop to consider what it must be like to live on the planet below, the purple glow of the immense phase coils like a new star that, through a quirk of phase physics, provides no heat. You conclude it must be more pleasant there than on the other end of the weapon. 

You cut the comm link.

Your $shipOrFleet maintains a safe distance from the immense construct, a spray of phase-active particle fluid surrounds it, producing a strangely beautiful effect similar to an intense magnetic field. While in theory harmless, your technical officer has advised staying outside the field until we know exactly what we want to accomplish with the object.

Neither Sensors nor Tactical are sure of exactly what to make of the construct. The technical specifications and manuals still available post-Collapse make no mention of anything like it, neither does the oral history of myth and secondary-culture that has grown around objects like Cryosleepers and Gatehaulers.

Your pondering of the object and its purpose is interrupted by an automated proximity warning klaxon. A fleet of Domain-era drone warships peel out from behind a cloud of debris and begin transmitting a message via tightbeam communications.

 "WARNING: This automated message speaks with the voice and authority of the Domain Ministry of Intelligence.

Attention citizen of the Domain, this automated drone ship has identified and logged your vessel or habitat trespassing in space claimed for use by the Domian Ministry of Intelligence. Your presence here violates the DOMINT Emergency Powers Act, the punishment for this infraction is severe, stand down and comply-. "

INTERRUPT

no prisoner capacity remaining. new directive. target must not reveal location. break target down for further defence fabrication.

As your $shipOrFleet finish mopping up the automated defences, a weak hyperwave ping is detected coming from the object. It's unclear if this is random noise from a dying subsystem or some kind of encrypted signal, sent to inform someone or something of our presence here.

Your $shipOrFleet continues toward the object without further incident.

Now closer to the object, scans make it abundantly clear that the failure of the immense phase coils was not a natural result of interstellar weathering, the outer hull is slaked with the telltale scars and craters of weapon impacts. Judging by the size, shape and other factors of the impact craters, it is determined the phase coils were targeted by the drone fleet in orbit in a deliberate act of sabotage. 

Given that it is clearly intended to be unmanned, the object makes a surprising number of unintended concessions to human occupation, while it has no internal atmosphere, scans indicate the majority of the structure is laced with a network of interconnected maintenance ducts. Large enough to accommodate the clunky and unwieldy Domain-era maintenance drones now very rarely seen in the modern sector, it would be trivial for a salvage team to navigate.

Your salvage teams dock shuttles at various entry points along the massive hull and fan out through the structure. Through reports that trickle up the hierarchy it becomes almost immediately apparent that the innards of the vast machine have been stripped of anything deemed non-essential by the drone defense fleet, nothing of any salvage value remains. Seeing that the next few hours will be mostly uneventful call and response, you zone out.

The impression of something not unlike distant music inserts itself into the gap in your consciousness, a choir of singers, beautiful yet abhorrent. Saccharine but sterile. When you attempt to focus on the music it slips away, sliding between space. You become suddenly aware that your bridge crew is staring at you expectantly, it is difficult to determine how much time passed.

"$PlayerSirOrMadam, we've found something." your operations chief states deadpan, clearly not the first time.

You review a ground-level feed from a salvor's suit cam. Probe-mounted radar starts to build a picture in your bridge display while suit lights pile their beams into the space, catching drifts of dust in what appears to be a well fortified server room. Some of the databanks are embossed with the logo of the Domain Ministry of Intelligence. 

Looking closer at the feed it becomes obvious that the room was originally designed for some purpose other than housing this datacentre. The databanks are provided for by haphazard cabling and power conduits that weave through holes made in the walls, ceiling and floor. 

"There are no access terminals a human operator could use, and even if there were, I wouldn't trust this setup." Continues your operations chief, "accessing the data would require transferring the entire datacentre to one of our ships."

After transferring the server room to your cargo hold, a task made surprisingly easy by the modularity of the Domain-era computers, you can finally access the data within. The integrity of the data is surprisingly high, the immense bulk of the megastructure clearly helped to shield the delicate computer systems from the long term affects of exposure to the failed phase field. You take a moment to ponder the fact that the moving of this datacentre may have already occurred, transferred from an installation somewhere else in system to an easily defensible position chosen by the drone fleet.

The data has been downloaded and placed in a secure cache for your review.

text:
The data within reveals an awful and incredible truth. Your $shipOrFleet is in orbit of an immense weapon, the enclosed specification describes it as a DISPP-974C Interfector, designed specifically to deliver a single payload without any possibility of interception, a dedicated Planetkiller Device Delivery Vehicle. It is a monument to death and madness, designed by Consolidated Mysore-Congreve under contract with the Domain Ministry of Intelligence, left here to rot by the corpse of the Domain post-Collapse, the Dead Hand having slipped off of The Button before it could fall to hit it. 

It is the ironically cold inverse of a Domain-era Cryosleeper. Rather than carrying hopeful colonists to new opportunities on the frontier of Domain space, it is the unseen shackle around those new polities, an unstated threat of instant and assured retribution against any polity that does not bend the knee to the great Domain of Man. 

Recovered - DISPP-974C Design Specifications

This blacksite, and the data implies that at least one such site exists for every sector of Domain space, was established shortly before the first recorded wave of colonisation in the Persean Sector. A crew of DOMINT engineers supported by a dedicated Explorarium Mothership were tasked with establishing an automated complex here in deep space capable of manufacturing, fueling and in theory deploying the DISPP-974C along with monitoring the local sector. 

A dedicated gate allows effective backdoor access to the Persean Sector, while an overtuned hyperwave communications relay allows for listening in on all interstellar communications within the Core Worlds. Well secluded, the Domain saw all.

Logs indicate that an immense Planetkiller Arsenal was at one point present in system. According to the specifications of the DISPP-974C, the hundreds of independently targetable submunitions within, each with their own Planetkiller Device payload, would allow a single missile to sunder the entirety of the Core Worlds within a cycle if deemed necessary.

It seems that by design, the crew were not self sufficient. To ensure loyalty no food was permitted to be produced in system, instead relying on resupply via the gate network. Stranded here in deep space with limited supplies post-Collapse, records indicate the crew enacted network failure protocol, as is standard of Domain military assets disconnected from command. Most of the crew were put into emergency cryosleep on the planet below, while more senior engineers worked to reprogram the defensive drones to ensure the secrecy of the operation. 

This override permitted the deconstruction of all "non-mission critical" material in the system to be repurposed into a defensive fleet. This fleet was ordered to intentionally sabotage the facility, destroying the immense phase coils and automated maintenance systems. Unfortunately for the survival of the DOMINT personnel this new Custodian Taskforce deemed the cryosleep pods "non-mission critical" and had them repurposed.

Logs indicate the Domain-era Mothership in system was tasked with dispersing the Planetkiller Arsenal, it seems likely the hyperwave signal sent by the station post battle was intended for this Mothership. Unfortunately without a lock on its trajectory this would be promising lead on a Planetkiller is practically cold from the outset. 

In a moment of incredible clarity you realise that like all hidden weapons, in being here away from the prying eyes of the Persean Sector rather than in public view, the DISPP-974C Interfector was denied its true potential as a potent symbol. 

Possessing this weapon, even if it isn't functional, is power in of itself. A threat of unavoidable retribution that would never need to come, the greatest bluff the Persean Sector has ever seen and the ultimate bargaining chip. It would be a gun pointed at the head of the Persean Sector, loaded with a blank.

"So. They were expecting to just get a crude map of where the nearby gates are, which they did of course, but they also found this," he taps at his datapad and holds it up to the holorecorder. The data displayed is made less legible by his inability to hold the datapad steady, likely jitters of excitement at doing something slightly rebellious, that or nerves. Your communications officer notes down the displayed coordinates.

"Wait what? R-really? Aw, then I guess our last hurrah is already over..." He looks visibly  disappointed, and then perks up, realising he will get the answers to his questions immediately. "What was there?" He asks excitedly.

Speaking about this at all is already going behind Provost Baird's back..." 

"Which I'm fine to do!" he quickly adds, "at least on this small scale, but... I like my job Captain." The prospect of losing this positon seems to genuinely upset him, even with the hazards it has come with.

"Oh." He looks more than a bit crestfallen, you get the distinct feeling you've ruined this reunion for him. He makes an effort to put on a smile, it's almost impressive how fake it looks. 

"Do let me know if you change your mind... You should already have everything you need anyway."

She smiles, self assured, "hence, over however many cycles it has been, we get a superorganism!"

text:
You convene your senior officers to discuss a ground insertion on $name. Both SIGINT and HUMINT are nonexistent, what with the lack of human opposition, so planning the operation is unorthodox. 

To the dismay of the marine company head, Nideliko has volunteered to assist from the ground. According to her analysis the superorganism should display no overt hostility towards the team. Weaponry, particularly of the antimatter family, will however be necessary to clear the path from the landing site to the Biofactory womb. 

A volley of precise orbital orbital burns from your $shipOrFleet excises a patch of slagged wasteland into the surface of $name, Sensors reports that the Biofactory is already growing back into the space, but it will be days before the landing site is retaken.

The contingent of marines and their Xenobiology escort are already on route. Bridge displays flicker with hundreds of vidfeeds, each accompanied by health monitors and antixenol dosage trackers. 

As promised, the operation is mostly uneventful, the occasional tunnels carved through the flesh slowly contract behind the team ominously, but no deliberate attempts are otherwise made by the superorganism to stop their advance. Progress is slow through the macroscale organs of the Biofactory, bicuspid valves larger than the company APCs slowly open and close off routes, releasing streams of synthetic compounds in their wake. 

Fronds of villi wave and cling to the combat suits of those at the edges of the pack, but seem otherwise harmless, pits of mucus and other fluids are occasionally waded through. After a few hours the team reach the formed ceramometal shells of a ruined human settlement, entwined within the embrace of the living landscape.

Nideliko's feed jitters slightly as she waits beside a genetics kit inside one of the APCs, the Tripad connected to the unit lights up red after roughly a minute to her profound disappointment. The Xenobiologist scrawls what you assume to be "Genetics too corrupted" with graphite before she slaps a hand against her suit faceplate and activates comms. 

"$PlayerSirOrMadam! Surface report! This site is a bust, the genetics are too corrupted by replication to be the origin. Moving on." She turns to face the marine company lead and the feed shakes left and right, they move out immediately.

A dedicated holo tracks the teams movements across the surface, by taking the path of least resistance through the tunnels it begins to appear disturbingly like a blood vessel chart. Within a few further hours the next remnant of human civilisation is reached, a ribcage of synthetic material for the synthetic organism.

This time the the Tripad lights a reassuring shade of green, to which Nideliko's feed jumps vertically slightly and clatters against the low roof of the transport vehicle. "Captain! Report! We are at the location, genetic corruption as low as 0.095%!" They seemingly begin talking to the surface team. "Spread out! The inner epidermis is somewhere here, once we breach the womb we can extract the Embryo." 

The operation moves quickly from there, a heavy antimatter weapon slices an entrance through a particularly suppurate layer of skinlike tissue, a pump is then used to drain the amniotic fluid and mucus disgorged from what you presume to be the Biofactory womb.

Ominous. And profoundly unhelpful, no records of such a thing exist."

"Then I was right Captain!" Nideliko exclaims, her cadence accelerating as she talks. "These nanites didn't have a chance-" she pauses for a microsecond. "Actually no. They didn't have a reason, to shut off post-Collpase, so they just kept fertilising the environment without anyone left to take in the harvest. Every cycle yet more organisms die and decay and eventually the ecosystem destabilised from the unsustainable rate of decomposition." 

She stops to breathe. "$name will eventually recover, granted we can find a way to shut them off, but the timescale of that recovery is likely thousands of cycles. The damage is functionally permanent." 

Sensors sees this conclusion as a fitting time to interject. "$PlayerSirOrMadam, we have a subsurface signal. Judging by the broadcast indicia its internal control comms, product designation is an EUT-202 Soil Nanite Web." They pull up a holo of $name, "it forwards to a ruined arcology complex for manual control, but we have no compatible recall codes on file."
options: jdp_soilNanitesTechnologyOpinion:"Could we somehow trip the failsafe?"

text:
The bridge goes silent for a moment, Technology brings up a logistics processing tool on their terminal. "Volatiles are certainly too difficult to handle," comes quietly, for themselves rather than you. "Transplutonics though..."

They look up from their station. "We would only need to saturate a comparatively small local volume." A quiet exhalation. "We can't be certain, the specs eschew specifics on the exact nature of the failsafe, but even a few individual nanites detecting the change should hopefully trigger a cascading recall order, Domain-era safeties tend to be draconian like that."

"It will be tough, but hypothetically if we can airdrop a sufficient amount of loose transplutonics on top of the arcology control centre, we should be able to trip the failsafe and collect the Soil Nanites for our own use."

"It can be done," your Operations Chief states, dry as Mairaath. "Planning and enacting a series of precise orbital drops, several hundred tonnes of hyperdense material in volume," they pause. "Its an immense logistical problem, but mechanically its very simple, functionally no different from a tactical antimatter bombardment," they nod to their left. "Tactical?" 

Tactical continues on cue, smooth and efficient, "indeed, and with no hostile defenses to evade, the optimal flight plans of our shuttles can be guided by the cold hand of orbital mechanics. Coordination can piggyback off of our military comms, the limiting factor will be the loading time. If we can't fill them quickly enough back at the $shipOrFleet it will massively slow us down."

text:

Loading will be slower, but even pessimistically I think it would only take a day to drop a few hundred tonnes with an expanded cargo crew." 

They pause, visibly thinking, "regarding the delivery, it would be be inaccurate but not uncontrollable. The material would however have an impact velocity high enough to embed itself in the surface."

Technology interjects, "which is in fact desirable! The deeper they are the closer the radiation source is to the nanite web and the higher the likelihood we will trip the failsafe," they stop. "This seems oddly achievable."

text:
"$PlayerSirOrMadam, we're getting a signal from the local volume. Faint, but definitely artificial." 

They pull a headset over their ears and flick a switch to begin streaming the signal. When questioned previously, sensors insisted that artificial signals are easier to hear than see. This explanation proved contentious with your technology officer.

"Angle suggests it's backscatter from a microsat. Comms between surface installations seems plausible. Composition is highly ordered and we have some geodetic coordinates encoded." 

They look puzzled for a moment. "Negative vertical datum, $PlayerSirOrMadam. Something deep beneath the surface? There's other data here I can't parse."
options: jdp_mantleBore1:"Tech, crack that signal. Sensors, get us a closer look."

text:
"Yes $PlayerSirOrMadam!" comes simultaneously. Technology pulls up a data analysis tool to begin trawling through a visualisation of the signal. It moves quickly, bright, flowing and arcane. "The human ear, incapable of decoding complex encryption? I would never have guessed."

Sensors, the very image of cool-headed professionalism, removes the headphones with more force than they are rated for.

"This was no fringe mining operation, Captain," they deflect, marking extensive bands of magrail on a holo of $name. "There's hundreds of dead mass drivers along the equator. This place must have experienced shipping traffic to rival Kazeron." 

With a flick of the wrist a series of standard surveyors probes are dispatched to the surface. You watch one impact through the scopes in a kick of dust, a spec of ultra-visibility yellow amongst the muted landscape. Grainy at first, the visual feed crystallises into an unremarkable patch of oxide sand.

As the data is picked through by the operations team in orbit, a holo of the arcology is annotated with POIs. An extensive executive cryosanctum is marked a few floors up from the team, while many times redundant nutrient cyclers and reactors appear in bands across the structure. "Seems like we have our operators." Technology concludes, "E.U.T.C. top brass. Some kind of specialist terraforming crew." 

The workers of the E.U.T.C. are legendary to some. Hero-Engineers who could beat and bend celestial spheres to their will. Coax and sculpt life from barren stone.

"From the logs we have a total of 50 individuals in suspension since pre-Collapse, but look here." They pull up the specs of a cryosanctum variant, marking some small indicia that match data from the complex. "This is a short-term suspension system." 

"Revival is meant to be much more pleasant, but it doesn't do the heavy lifting to maintain the body for long periods, the longest safe sleep cycle lasts about a year. Its designed for this kind of team, valuable people working on long term projects. They set up a system, sleep until it does its job, and then wake up to do the next. Preserves their lifespan."

"The safety has been exceeded by hundreds of cycles..." They spool through logs for a moment and make a sound of relief. "Diagnostics indicate life signs from all 50 pods, but in terrible shape, they'll need intensive medical." 

They smile a vicious ex-Tri-Tacyhon smile. "On the bright side, they should be pretty agreeable in regards to operating the MCO Unit if we save their lives."

text:
You convene your senior officers to discuss reviving the E.UT.C. team. The atmosphere of $name is breathable and the arcology surprisingly well sealed. The planned surgeries are complex even without the expected complications, but your Chief Medical Officer is confident full revival is achievable entirely within the complex. 

A medical bay in the $shipOrFleet is disassembled, its occupants shuffled, their dismay ignored, and its equipment compacted for transport.

Cooled crates of organs, pallets of medical technology and a cocktail of heavy duty sedatives are all moved through the complex, locations tracked by a series of holos and vidfeeds. A makeshift medical bay assembles within the cryosanctum in real time, medical aids preparing tools and beds and displays. The crew give the cryosanctum one last disinfection, a task spacers often perform compulsively regardless, and the surgical teams are ready to begin.

The revival is a long and arduous process. Countless biometrics are meticulously monitored during each wakeup cycle to quickly determine where the sleepers body will begin to unravel first. The effects of long-term unmaintained cryosleep are more visceral than you imagined, and after the first dozen operations you decidedly stop watching. 

Logs indicate the medical team switched with their backups 19 times over the course of 3 shifts, a marathon of work that deserves commendation. At present the medical readout shows all 50 sleepers green.

You request a commlink with your Chief Medical Officer and they preempt your question deftly. "The last sleeper will wake from anaesthesia by end of next shift, $PlayerSirOrMadam. The best course of action from a psychological shock perspective is to have them awaken in the environment they expect. I recommend the senior staff join us here on the surface to ask any questions."
options: jdp_mantleBoreMedicalOperation3:"Agreed. XO, you have the conn."

text:
You leave operational command to your XO and pile into a shuttle with your most senior bridge staff. A short trip and transfer to a rover later, you are greeted by your Chief Medical Officer in the cryosanctum recovery wing. 

A number of sleepers are awake but paralysed, scrolling through a post-Collapse primer with little flits of eye movement. 

"We've asked a few questions already". They look down at their Tri-Pad for a name, "Executive-Engineer Rulison Plowshare, that was it, is the team lead. They're awake but immobile, speech returned about ten minutes ago. From my assessment they were high on the E.U.T.C. corporate ladder, but I never was one for office politics or history."

A medical aide escorts you to the bedside of one Rulison Plowshare, immobile but lucid. Your first impression is of visual paradox. A working spacers suit, vivisected and resealed to access targeted organs, is worn with a luxury handweave shawl. The well groomed face of an Executive looks at you through the robust and practical implants of an engineer. 

When he speaks it is clearly difficult, through the lethargic vocal chords and paralysed muscles of a man barely revived. 

When they survive the arduous conversion from thought to vibrational wave, the words arrive with the slant of accent you cannot place. Perhaps the dialect of some lost E.U.T.C. subculture. Dead. Along with the rest of the company.

"You aren't with us, are you?" comes with some difficulty.

They chuckle slightly, an unpleasant sound following from their lungs as they nearly choke on the prospect. An attendant from your medical staff moves Rulison to an upright position before retreating behind some sterilised privacy sheeting.

"I thought as much. I've been reading." 

They flick their eyes down to a Tri-Pad. "It seems me and mine are a dead kind." They strain their partially paralysed facial muscles into half a smile. "The work of centuries, undone and co-opted and mocked. I saw the beginning, now I sit here, at the end." 

"You don't even know Assuwa, not by that name."

"Assuwa" he replies, and waits to imbue some majesty into his words. It is as if the need to share his history overpowers the anaesthesia. His speaking becomes less laboured, pride seeping into his voice. And anger, and melancholy.

"The Assuwa system. Our finest work... My finest work". They strain to point a hand to their chest, "eco-design lead for Karkiya, until the arrival of the agitator monks had me and mine reassigned out here as mining technicians." Their tone becomes slightly mocking, the universal signifier of imitating someone not present. "Too valuable of an asset to risk during the unrest." 

They pause, considering something. "I suppose that was the right move, in the end. Most of the work was done, and my time there was fulfilling."

"Your history calls it Gilead now. Ugly name for a beautiful place."
options:
jdp_mantleBoreRulisonDontKnow:"I. I don't know what to say."
jdp_mantleBoreRulisonGilead:"You did a great service. Gilead is a Jewel."
jdp_mantleBoreRulisonKarkiya:"You did a great service. Karkiya is a Jewel."

text: He smiles. "You don't need to say anything. This is my grudge to keep."

If he begrudges you using the Luddic name, he doesn't really show it. Perhaps it would color his expression with a tighter control of his facial muscles. "Gilead" he sighs. 

"Thank you. It was good work, proud work."

He smiles. "Thank you." 

A low chuckle starts in his chest, and grows into full, vaguely manic laughter. You worry for a moment that he may shake his fragile body apart. "I guess all I have to do is spread the good word, like this Ludd fellow, and the true name shall be adopted by its own evident virtue."

He moves his hand from his chest, and you suddenly notice that he hadn't done it sooner. "Now I'm no fool. You haven't saved me and mine purely out of kindness." He stops, "and even if you had, I owe you." 

His eye flits down to the Tri-Pad, searching it for a moment before making an admirable attempt to meet your gaze, neck frozen by a chemical cocktail illegal in most of the Sector. "What is it you need from me, Captain $playerName?"
options: jdp_mantleBoreRulisonOverride:"The MCO Unit, are you licensed?"

text:
"For the bore?" he asks, and gleans the answer from your face. "I am. Not that it matters now. Your pamphlet said the gates are dead, so it's useless."

He notices your confusion, "the database of licensed operators is stored on Eridani II, nonsense Domain restriction to prevent tampering. Slowed down the work a thousand-fold, so," the vestiges of a smirk makes its way onto his face, like a child confessing to stealing rations, "we would queue hundreds of cycles worth of commands at once, and just cancel what we didn't want later. That's why it's still going." 

"My biometrics are on the list, but without couriers going back and forth it isn't worth a scrip. Unfortunately for you, there are only two options, and only one good one. It either stays doing what its doing, wasted work for nobody for the next hundred cycles, or we recall it." 

"That doesn't require authorization of course," he smiles, slightly saccharine. "For safety."

Before you can move, your technology officer pushes through the privacy sheet, speed enough to leave it to flapping behind them. "I knew there must be a reason they all failed with the Collapse!"

Rulison looks at them, bewilderment in their eyes if not on their face. Technology pokes their head back through the sheeting and calls out to your Operations Chief, "Ops! The override is dead! We have to recall the bore manually! Stand by for instructions!"

You hear a medical aide quiet them rather pointedly, and they motion apologetically through the sheeting. They turn to face you with their body but occupy their eyes with a Tri-Pad. After a few moments they look up. "T-minus 14 minutes Captain, recall order was received by the bore and it is breaching as we speak. Ops projects it will be secured in the hold within the hour."

Rulison looks slightly apologetic. "Captain. It may seem to you an odd request, but... I need to do more than that. That was nothing, I just gave you information." 

He takes a moment, likely to consider his words. "Me and mine are talented folk. Skilled technicians, engineers, ecologists, logisticians. All of us." They look down at the Tri-Pad again. "200 cycles is a long time $playerName, for you to be the first face I see... That bodes poorly for our prospects. It seems to me our trade is a dying one."

"Our triumphs have been attributed to the divine, us mere mortals are inconvenient."

"I won't see another face, not before we run out of supplies. I figure we leave with you, or not at all." He pauses. "We do good work, we would be proud to make miracles again."

That these mere mortals are in dire need of a new contract is left hanging, a silent thread running through the entire conversation.
options: jdp_mantleBoreRulisonDisplay:"What can you do? Practically speaking."

text: Rulison clearly enjoys talking about his work, the conversation moves effortlessly. You determine quickly that him and his team easily eclipse the terraforming state of the art in the Sector.
options:
jdp_mantleBoreRulisonHire:Hire Rulison Plowshare
jdp_mantleBoreRulisonCore:Offer transport to the core

text:
Through tiny movements of the eyes and shoulders you get the impression of an immense weight lifting from Rulison's shoulders. You had never seen him without it until now, but the way he was moments ago feels unnatural in comparison. 

They just secured a paycheck and work for 'them and theirs' in the wake of the end of the world. Looking out for your crew in hard times is a common spacer virtue, you can respect it.

"Thank you, Captain. Proud to be of service."

After brief pleasantries with Rulison you and your senior staff return to the $shipOrFleet. The E.U.T.C. team are retrieved in groups via shuttle as recovery schedules permit. Within the shift the makeshift medical bay is dismantled and all crew are accounted for.

The bore, dredged up from where it beached itself upon a plateau of glassed earth by an ultra-heavy lifting shuttle, was safely secured in the $shipOrFleets hold in your absence.

notes: # aka the "Oneslaught" :D -dgb

text: At first it appears to be a rather boring find, no doubt one of countless Merucry-class shuttles ambushed by pirates for their passengers ransom. Then you begin to doubt.
The executive shuttle drifts slowly, without weapons it was likely used to more company than just rocks, but they seem to have protected it all the same. Until we arrived at least.

Your sensors officer begins a preliminary scan of the ship, the first inconsistencies are flagged immediately by mere visual inspection. 

Even weathered by cycles of radiation the livery is unmistakeable. The myriad blue-green hues represent the long defunct Eridani-Utopia Terraforming Corporation. This ship has likely been here for quite a while. 

Unusual, given its proximity to the core. Perhaps the modest asteroid field shielded it from sensors.

The first salvage team moves in to sweep the shuttle, docking at the small drone bay usually converted to house weapon feedlines by the ship's more contemporary cousins. 

The lack of weaponry is technically not unusual for a Merury-class shuttle, but the modern socio-economic climate quite firmly insists upon their aftermarket installation.

The movement of the teams tools into the bay is hindered by an intricate network of surveying probes and single-occupant shuttles, fading into the darkness of the bay. 

Power from a portable reactor is fed to the ship's core systems through a series of modular inlets. Emergency lighting flickers on accompanied with a low humming through the suits external microphones. The extent of the stored equipment is quite staggering.

Your technical officer begins spooling through recorded hullspecs and hums in affirmation with themself. "This isn't standard spec, $PlayerSirOrMadam. Some kind of aftermarket surveying grid. Likely didn't come cheap, and probably not something anyone still around could pull off."

Surveying equipment of one family is shimmied carefully past that of the other. The feed from the lead salvor's suit cam shimmers slightly as it is re-routed through the ship's own systems, ready for deeper exploration.

Cables are run and drones deployed, the team moves to the first bulkhead and meets uncharacteristic resistance. "Proper reinforcement" your ops chief states dismissively. "The people this thing carried were ransomable."

Progress is slow, but after a few shifts each with the cutting torch the team breach the interior. The sliced bulkhead is a portal to luxury unrivalled. 

Fine wood panelling lines every surface, intricate crystalline lighting systems float in zero-gravity near the ceiling, likely intended to hang and scatter light and delight. The deckplates are covered by carpets in the company colors. 

Hand painted landscapes are framed in what you assume to be the entrance hallway. You recognise one from a holo as the surface of Gilead - with significantly fewer Luddic sites - and realise they are likely all real locations sculpted by the EUTC.

Some of the closer extravagances have been melted away by the heat of the torch, blackened or otherwise congealed into an alloyed mass. Your ops chief almost recoils from the feed, warded away by the sheer gaudiness. "Very ransomable."
options:
jdp_eridaniWreckExploreDisgusting:"Disgusting decor. They had terrible taste"
jdp_eridaniWreckExploreImpractical:"How fundamentally wasteful..."
jdp_eridaniWreckExploreBrilliant:"It's brilliant. What a beautiful ship."

text: Someone behind you stifles their amusement.
Your ops chief grunts in agreement.
Your ops chief glares at you with the intensity of a high intensity laser.

The team moves in deeper. Navigation is aided by a series of 'subtle' decals, tracing lines along the wooden wall panels to key locations. The concept is not unfamiliar to the internal design of a warship, but it is accomplished with profoundly impractical gold trim.

Further exploration is mostly uneventful, beyond the novelty of encountering the skeleton of some long deceased aquatic mammal in a drained aquarium. The bridge is reached within the hour.

An obsidian plaque designates the ship as the EUTS Intelligent Designer. The contents of a recovered blackbox datacore are transmitted to the $shipOrFleet and your technical staff begin unpicking the vessels history.

Employed by the terraforming company for hundreds of cycles leading up to the Collapse - and pointedly fewer cycles immediately after - navigation logs indicate the ship was a transport for high priority personnel between the companies expected haunts. 

Some flightplan coordinates match with Corvus, Canaan, and Penelope's Star at first glance, but there are a dozen logged trips each cycle of the vessels extensive history. Your technology officer pulls together a quick script to sort the data, talking through the output as it runs. 

"Yma and Isirah were visited quite a lot 'more recently'," they gesture quotations as they speak. "But that was still over a hundred and fifty cycles ago. The last logged location is here, Penelope. A shortlived combat log implies they got jumped by the Luddic Church without escort a short distance out from Ithaca."
options: jdp_eridaniWreckExplore5:"Ithaca... So how did they end up out here?"

text:
Your tactical officer interjects. "I see two options, $PlayerSirOrMadam. They could have fled combat and hid here to avoid detection, or the Knights towed them here to hide evidence of the battle. Without a proper forensic investigation we have no way to be sure."

Technical chuckles. "Maybe the Chruch will tell if we just ask nicely." 

"Regardless." They continue, "we have a few interesting hits." A map of the sector streams to the central display. The logged coordinates are plotted as a heatmap and the core glows bright with the presence of known and invariably cancelled terraforming projects. "We know all the obvious ones, but look here, these systems on the fringe."

Three systems, frequented by Eridani-Utopia, none currently known to host organised polities.
options: jdp_eridaniWreckExplore6:"Terraformed worlds, out there for the taking?"

Without stabilisation the $jdp_market Array will deorbit within days, projections of the deaths to follow are invariably bleak. Models of the predicted impact sites, ecosystem destabilisation, traffic disruption, civil unrest and more spool on your console.

"$PlayerSirOrMadam, we can't do nothing. Can we?" comes from a junior officer, slightly meek. You realise in that moment it is the first time you have ever heard them speak, their life, like so many in your hands never given a second thought.

text:
The tension on the bridge is deftly cut by the prospect of action, plans and contingencies are the opiate of spacers. "Yes $playerSirOrMadam! Opening channel..." Comms manipulates their suite and clicks their tongue. "We have a secure link to detonator control, forwarding now." 

The mundane interface that unfolds on your console obfuscates the scale of your preparation. Tonnes of antimatter fuel stringed across each component of the $jdp_market Array, primed to annihilate the entire structure at your input.

There is a certain melancholy in destroying this feat of engineering, a miracle unprecedented post-Collapse, but its existence proves that it can and will again be achieved.

Your command interface blinks a biometric scan and asks only one thing. DETONATE?

Rulison Plowshare sits behind the faux-arbor desk of a modest office, likely in the bowels of whatever bureaucratic centre exists on a Qaras. The planet and its lone orbital shade are rendered in miniature by a holo between him and the source of the vidfeed. It obscures his face for a moment before collapsing away into the projector.

"Captain $playerName. What can I do for you"
options:
jdp_rulisonQaras1:"I trust you are still on retainer?"

text:
His face breaks into a smile. "Sure am, I take you considered the proposal?" 

He looks to the side, vaguely secretive, and an exertion of the shoulder suggests flicking a switch beneath the desk, likely a privacy filter. 

"To be candid, $playerName. We are not appreciated here. I'm sure you are aware, new management came in some time ago. Surviviors from our top-brass are few in number, and lacking in ambition."

"We have work, the shade won't fall on our watch, that is certain, but some of us are wanting for more, understand? The transition wouldn't be maligned by the crew, just say the word and we'll be ready within a day."
options: jdp_rulisonQaras2:"Remind me, what can you do? Practically speaking."

text: Rulison clearly enjoys talking about his work, the conversation moves effortlessly. As he speaks you begin to recall the details of your previous assessment. Him and his team easily eclipse the terraforming state of the art in the Sector.

text:
Rulsion betrays any potential non-compete clause in his previous contract immediately and ruthlessly, opening a series of commlinks to his team. The office becomes akin to your bridge, a warroom of industrial espionage. Countless faces, some you recognise from the beds of the recovery room and others not, materialise, listen to your terms relayed through Rulison, and vanish. In all, 49 accept, but by your count at least 80 were asked.

"We picked up some new folks" he explains. "Not as loyal." He begins moving around the room, collecting objects and dismissing holos. "Or more loyal. Depends how you figure I suppose." 

"We're keeping everyone who matters". A quick movement of the wrist sends the coordinates of a less reputable spacedock to your Tri-Pad. Within the shift Rulison and his team are safely aboard your $shipOrFleet. 

"Thank you, Captain. Proud to be of service."

The purple emblem of the Domain Sixth Battlegroup performs half a rotation. After a short wait, your connection request is denied. 

To see the silver amphiptere attached to piracy is not uncommon, but its implications are clear. This station was once the haunt of Warlord Leonis, inheriting the comms frequencies he himself inherited from the Domain.
